title: MRI Biomarkers for Brain Metastases in Lung Cancer Using Machine Learning
abstract: Purpose Existing prognostic models for brain metastases from lung cancer rely on clinical variables and do not capture the biological heterogeneity of host or tumor factors underlying survival outcomes. We evaluated whether MRI-derived radiomic biomarkers improve prognostic stratification beyond clinical variables. We also investigated their biological correlates using matched histopathology. Experimental Design This retrospective study included 103 patients with brain metastases from lung cancer and matched pre-operative MRI and histopathology. Radiomic features from T1-weighted contrast-enhanced and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were combined with clinical variables to train Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and DeepSurv models for overall survival (OS), CNS progression, and leptomeningeal (LM) progression. Risk groups from an imaging-only model were compared for clinical and histopathologic differences. Results Imaging features improved prognostic performance beyond clinical variables across all modeling frameworks, with the combined clinical-imaging DeepSurv model achieving the highest concordance index for OS (0.728). Risk groups from the best-performing model for each endpoint differed significantly in OS (median 26.7 vs. 9.1 months, p < 0.001) and LM progression ( p = 0.003), but not in CNS progression. Imaging-only risk groups did not differ significantly in any clinical variable, but high-risk patients were less likely to have tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (46% vs. 77%, p = 0.010) and PD-L1 expression ≥ 50% (10% vs. 32%, p = 0.049). Conclusions MRI radiomic biomarkers provide prognostic information beyond established clinical variables in lung cancer brain metastases and correspond to features of the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting their potential to refine risk stratification. Statement of Translational Relevance Brain metastases affect 30-40% of patients with lung cancer. Existing prognostic models rely on clinical variables, which do not fully capture the biological heterogeneity that drives outcomes. We show that machine learning models integrating MRI-derived radiomic features with clinical variables improve prognostic discrimination beyond clinical variables alone. Because these biomarkers are derived from standard-of-care pre-operative imaging, they can be generated without additional testing or delay to treatment planning. Using matched histopathology from resected lesions, we further show that imaging-defined risk groups do not simply reproduce established clinical risk factors but instead correspond to differences in the tumor immune microenvironment, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression. These findings support the use of quantitative imaging biomarkers as a non-invasive method to refine risk stratification at diagnosis, informing treatment selection and clinical trial enrollment for patients with brain metastases from lung cancer.

Purpose

Existing prognostic models for brain metastases from lung cancer rely on clinical variables and do not capture the biological heterogeneity of host or tumor factors underlying survival outcomes. We evaluated whether MRI-derived radiomic biomarkers improve prognostic stratification beyond clinical variables. We also investigated their biological correlates using matched histopathology.

Experimental Design

This retrospective study included 103 patients with brain metastases from lung cancer and matched pre-operative MRI and histopathology. Radiomic features from T1-weighted contrast-enhanced and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were combined with clinical variables to train Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and DeepSurv models for overall survival (OS), CNS progression, and leptomeningeal (LM) progression. Risk groups from an imaging-only model were compared for clinical and histopathologic differences.

Results

Imaging features improved prognostic performance beyond clinical variables across all modeling frameworks, with the combined clinical-imaging DeepSurv model achieving the highest concordance index for OS (0.728). Risk groups from the best-performing model for each endpoint differed significantly in OS (median 26.7 vs. 9.1 months, p < 0.001) and LM progression ( p = 0.003), but not in CNS progression. Imaging-only risk groups did not differ significantly in any clinical variable, but high-risk patients were less likely to have tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (46% vs. 77%, p = 0.010) and PD-L1 expression ≥ 50% (10% vs. 32%, p = 0.049).

Conclusions

MRI radiomic biomarkers provide prognostic information beyond established clinical variables in lung cancer brain metastases and correspond to features of the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting their potential to refine risk stratification.

Statement of Translational Relevance

Brain metastases affect 30-40% of patients with lung cancer. Existing prognostic models rely on clinical variables, which do not fully capture the biological heterogeneity that drives outcomes. We show that machine learning models integrating MRI-derived radiomic features with clinical variables improve prognostic discrimination beyond clinical variables alone. Because these biomarkers are derived from standard-of-care pre-operative imaging, they can be generated without additional testing or delay to treatment planning. Using matched histopathology from resected lesions, we further show that imaging-defined risk groups do not simply reproduce established clinical risk factors but instead correspond to differences in the tumor immune microenvironment, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression. These findings support the use of quantitative imaging biomarkers as a non-invasive method to refine risk stratification at diagnosis, informing treatment selection and clinical trial enrollment for patients with brain metastases from lung cancer.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Modeling to Aid in the Identification of Genetic Conditions in Infants with Congenital Heart Disease
abstract: Background: Genetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions. Methods: Retrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals. Results: The cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]). Conclusions: Routine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

title: Regime-Aware Router Learning for Multi-Domain Medical Image Generation with Diffusion Experts
abstract: Heterogeneous medical image data motivate domain-specialized diffusion experts, but expert specialization alone does not determine how their predictions should be combined during sampling. Learning a global router is particularly challenging when the server has limited, potentially unrepresentative images. We study two router-learning strategies for a fixed expert pool. Server-Only learns input- and timestep-dependent expert assignments from server images with component labels. Anchor-Delta (AD) uses the same images and frozen experts to obtain additional evidence from denoising losses. It distills targets that combine this evidence with the current router's assignments, while a proxy gate controls a subsequent refinement step. Component labels describe data origin; expert losses measure empirical prediction performance. We evaluate these distinct signals through routing analyses and paired medical image generation. An AD-trained router improves generation metrics over Server-Only in a heterogeneous four-domain setting, and a separate server-data study shows gains in held-out routing over a corrected-routing comparator. Additional paired evaluations show that the effect of inference-time evidence mixing varies across benchmarks. These findings establish server-data availability and expert performance as distinct considerations in learning routers for multi-domain diffusion models.

title: A Concept-informed Interpretable Artificial Intelligence Framework for Breast Ultrasound Diagnosis
abstract: Most existing artificial intelligence systems for breast ultrasound rely primarily on image-driven prediction, with limited incorporation of the knowledge from the Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) and the intermediate assessment processes underlying radiologists' workflow, thereby constraining their interpretability and alignment with clinical practice. We curated, to our knowledge, the largest multicenter collection of breast ultrasound images paired with structured BI-RADS descriptors, comprising 9,941 patients across 20 independent datasets. Across 14 testing datasets, IBUS demonstrated consistent generalization performance across different clinical centers and imaging conditions. Incorporating BI-RADS descriptors enabled fine-grained risk stratification, while cross-checking predicted BI-RADS grades against malignancy probabilities identified internally discordant predictions that may warrant additional clinical review. In a reader study involving eight radiologists, IBUS assistance increased diagnostic sensitivity among both junior and senior readers, with the potential of guiding radiologists to make targeted revision in risk stratification. Overall, IBUS exhibits its potential as a second-stage decision-support system that complements radiologists by providing additional risk estimates and interpretable evidence for diagnostically challenging cases. The demo video of IBUS platform is publicly available at https://github.com/zsz1997/IBUS.

title: Explicitly Aligned Multi-View Breast Cancer Risk Prediction from Variable-Length Screening Histories
abstract: Accurate breast cancer risk prediction from screening mammography is essential for improved risk stratification and personalized screening. It can benefit from both temporal breast tissue changes across longitudinal examinations and complementary anatomical information from craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views. Leveraging longitudinal information requires identifying corresponding tissue regions across examinations, yet most approaches rely on implicit feature alignment without explicitly enforcing spatial consistency. Recent work has demonstrated the benefits of explicit temporal alignment; however, existing methods model each view independently, preventing them from exploiting complementary CC and MLO information. Furthermore, explicit approaches have been limited to a single prior examination. To fill these gaps, we propose (github.com/sot176/FlexLMV-Net), a breast-wise longitudinal multi-view framework that jointly models CC and MLO views across screening examinations while accommodating a variable number of prior examinations. FlexLMV-Net explicitly aligns longitudinal feature maps and integrates complementary views through cross-view temporal fusion and a dual-stream attention block. Evaluated on EMBED and CSAW-CC, FlexLMV-Net consistently outperforms existing approaches across breast density, cancer subtypes, and demographic subgroups, highlighting the benefits of explicit longitudinal alignment, multi-view modeling, and flexible use of available screening history. We further introduce (github.com/sot176/BCRBench), an open-source benchmark that unifies state-of-the-art single- and multi-timepoint breast cancer risk prediction models under standardized preprocessing, training, inference, and evaluation protocols, enabling fair and reproducible comparison of existing methods.

title: NoduleFlow: Automatic 3D Lung Nodule Detection and Segmentation
abstract: Low dose Computed Tomography (CT) is the standard imaging modality for lung cancer screening. On CT scans, lung cancer typically manifests as pulmonary nodules, whose manual identification is time-consuming and prone to observer variability, image quality limitations, and suboptimal reading conditions. Moreover, subtle temporal changes are often difficult to quantify reliably in CT scans from the same patient across follow-up examinations. Deep learning-based approaches for the automatic detection and segmentation of lung nodules have demonstrated improved accuracy and efficiency. However, most existing approaches provide only coarse region-of-interest localisation, rely on prior lesion annotations or human supervision, or treat detection and segmentation as separate tasks. In this work, we present NoduleFlow, a framework for lung nodule detection, classification, and segmentation directly from series of CT volumes. Our proposal consists of four interconnected modules and operates in an automated manner at inference time, without requiring prior lesion annotations, manual initialisation, or region-of-interest pre-selection. We further investigate whether nodule localization benefits from the propagation of candidate regions across follow-up scans through inter-scan registration fields, as opposed to conventional independent per-scan analysis. The generalisability of the framework is systematically evaluated across four independent datasets. The results underscore the potential of automated pipelines for lung nodule analysis in screening and diagnostic settings.

title: Neuromorphic Decoding and Dynamical Image Reconstruction from Populations of Spiking Retinal Ganglion Cells
abstract: Decoding visual stimuli from the spiking activity of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) informs both our understanding of the retinal code and the design of visual prostheses. Natural vision is dynamic, yet state-of-the-art decoders mostly reconstruct single frames with artificial neural networks that process dense, continuous-valued signals rather than the retina's sparse, asynchronous spikes. We asked whether dynamic scenes can be reconstructed and tracked entirely within the spike domain, and at what computational cost. We built an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) whose neurons integrate the recorded RGC spikes over time. Populations of up to 1836 RGCs were recorded ex vivo from mouse retina on high-density microelectrode arrays while flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings and randomly moving handwritten digits were presented. For moving digits, one shared spiking encoder fed two readouts, one reconstructing the image and one decoding the digit's position. Compute energy was estimated from counted synaptic operations. The SNN decoded what and where at once. It reconstructed the stimuli with a structural similarity (SSIM) of up to 0.93, refining the reconstruction as spikes accumulated, and tracked a randomly moving target with a mean error of 1.33 pixels on a $32\times32$ grid. Its fidelity nearly matched that of the best of 17 larger spiking and artificial decoders (5.9 million to 1.7 billion parameters, versus 5.4 million), and at a mean firing rate of 14.2% it needed an estimated $\sim$70-fold less compute energy than a dense artificial network of the same architecture. Dynamic visual scenes can thus be decoded from retinal population activity in the spike domain, with a compact network and at a compute cost compatible with implantable and wearable neural interfaces, supporting spike-native decoders for visual prostheses.

title: MID: Mask-Image Distributional Divergence for Evaluating Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Current evaluation protocols for medical image segmentation remain largely anchored in sample-wise comparisons, e.g., Dice and Hausdorff distance, which require each prediction to be paired with a ground-truth mask. Yet two limitations arise in practice: they are inapplicable when predictions are made on unlabeled data; and even when annotations are available, they cannot assess whether a collection of predictions matches the distributional structure of the ground-truth population. We introduce MID (Mask-Image Distributional Divergence), a distribution-level evaluation metric for medical image segmentation. MID builds upon the observation that segmentation quality is a property of the joint image-mask distribution: a mask may be anatomically plausible in isolation yet incorrect for the image it accompanies. MID compares the joint distribution of images and masks between a reference set and a set of predictions, without requiring sample-wise correspondence. This captures both mask realism and image-mask consistency. We evaluate MID across 13 publicly available datasets spanning CT, MRI, and MRA. Under anatomically realistic corruptions across 56 organ groups, MID tracks mean Dice and Hausdorff distance without per-sample ground-truth pairing. MID also detects distributional shifts across modalities and anatomies, identifies image-mask misalignment through controlled shuffling experiments, and produces reliable model rankings across real segmentation models. Official implementation available at github.com/erc-caravel/pytorch-mid

title: Multiple classification of childhood and juvenile autism spectrum disorder from ABIDE-II sMRI using BN-GO-CNN.
abstract: Objectives Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) shows heterogeneous neurodevelopmental patterns across childhood, juvenile development, and adulthood, so binary MRI classification may not fully capture age-and sex-related variation. This study proposes a proof-of-concept framework for multiple classification using ABIDE-II T1-weighted structural MRI (sMRI). Methods After image-quality screening, sMRI slices were processed using Canny edge detection, brain-region cropping, 224 × 224 resizing, and augmentation. Images were organized into sex-based four-class, age-based four-class, and combined age-and-sex eight-class datasets, separating child, young, juvenile, adult, male, and female groups. A Batch-Normalized Grid-Optimized CNN (BN-GO-CNN) was developed to learn structural representations directly from preprocessed sMRI, with grid search used to select key CNN hyperparameters. The model was compared with VGG16, DenseNet201, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-B0 using identical image partitions. Results BN-GO-CNN achieved validation accuracies of 67.0 %, 64.0 %, and 60.5 % for sex-based, age-based, and combined age-and-sex classification, respectively. These outcomes remained above chance but showed limited class separability. Conclusions The modest performance suggests that label-related sMRI differences are subtle, supporting this framework as a preliminary test of CNN-assisted sMRI classification for future research use rather than a clinically reliable ASD diagnostic system.

title: Deco-CLIP: Dual-Branch Feature Decoupling CLIP for Fine-Grained Zero-Shot Medical Image Analysis
abstract: Abstract The CLIP model has been widely used in the medical field, improving the efficiency of disease screening and diagnosis by establishing feature-level associations between medical images and radiology reports. However, we have found that the contrastive learning strategy of current medical CLIP primarily focuses on distinguishing high-level semantic features. Therefore, it fails to capture the low-level features related to attributes and relational information, limiting performance in fine-grained tasks. To address these limitations, we propose Deco-CLIP to decouple representational features from semantic features. Specifically, the image modality consists of two Vision Transformer (ViT) encoders that extract semantic and texture features using different pretraining strategies. The text modality consists of a text encoder with dual branches to focus on tokens representing high- and low-level features. Furthermore, to enhance the model's ability to capture fine-grained features, we propose a threshold-adaptive sample mining strategy based on intra-modal similarity, which clusters semantically similar samples into mini-batches. Then, secondary contrastive learning is applied within the mini-batch to align the fine-grained features between image and text modalities. Additionally, a regularized attention mechanism is proposed to guide the two branches of the text encoder to focus on distinct feature representations. We evaluated Deco-CLIP on fine-grained zero-shot tasks, including multi-abnormality detection and report-to-volume retrieval. The results showed a 10.2\% improvement in accuracy for multi-abnormality detection and a 16.2\% increase in recall for report-to-volume retrieval, demonstrating the effectiveness of Deco-CLIP in fine-grained medical tasks. The code will be publicly released.

title: The Saturation Gap as a Diagnostic Clue for Methemoglobinemia in a Child with Persistent Low Oxygen Saturation
abstract: Abstract Background Persistent low peripheral oxygen saturation in children commonly prompts investigation for pulmonary or cardiovascular disease. However, when oxygen desaturation persists despite an unrevealing cardiopulmonary evaluation, dyshemoglobinemia should be considered. Case presentation We report the case of a 7-year-old girl with persistent low peripheral oxygen saturation for approximately five years. Her peripheral oxygen saturation remained between 85% and 89% on room air despite an otherwise normal clinical condition. Extensive investigations, including echocardiography, contrast echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography angiography, chest computed tomography, pulmonary function testing, and neurologic evaluation, did not identify a cardiopulmonary cause for the low oxygen saturation. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated a preserved partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO₂) of 115 mmHg on room air, increasing to 165 mmHg during a hyperoxia test. The calculated alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient was 2.3 mmHg. The discrepancy between the low pulse oximetry readings and preserved PaO₂ prompted evaluation for a dyshemoglobinemia. Co-oximetry demonstrated a methemoglobin level of 15%, supporting the diagnosis of methemoglobinemia. Conclusions Methemoglobinemia should be considered in children with persistent low peripheral oxygen saturation that is disproportionate to their clinical condition and cardiopulmonary findings. Recognition of a discrepancy between pulse oximetry and arterial oxygenation can provide an important diagnostic clue and may help prevent prolonged and unnecessary investigations.

title: ATLAS: Development and Evaluation of an AI -Enabled Framework for Anatomically Traceable Measurement Assurance in Fetal-Head Ultrasound Biometry
abstract: Abstract Background Fetal-head biometry is important for estimating gestational age, monitoring fetal development, and identifying abnormalities. As AI-enabled ultrasound systems become more prevalent, automated measurements may appear credible even with mislocalization, suboptimal imaging planes, or absent anatomical landmarks. Clinicians may receive measurements without adequate evidence on their origin or reliability. ATLAS is designed as an evidence-traceable framework to establish conditions for valid measurements. Methods ATLAS consists of a data integrity layer, Find, Confirm, and Measure. The integrity layer performs dataset-agnostic checks for image validity, label consistency, and patient-exclusive partitioning. Find localizes the fetal cranial region; Confirm verifies the anatomical structures required for valid biometry. Measure calculates biparietal diameter, occipitofrontal diameter, and head circumference using two methods: a deterministic localization geometry and a learned segmentation. Training used 3,790 eligible frames from 1,840 patients from public hospital-derived HC18/FETAL_PLANES_DB resources, with patient-exclusive training, validation, and testing; external evaluation used FP (880 frames/460 subjects) and UCL (55/15) cohorts. Outcomes were localization, CSP/LV evidence, and biometric error. Performance measures included availability/IoU, F1, mean absolute error, signed error, and prespecified joint BPD/HC tolerance. Site-specific adaptation and data-free parameter aggregation were added as secondary technical analyses for future edge deployment. Results Under controlled data-fault tests, the data integrity layer detected every introduced defect. Internal validation demonstrated that Find localized all frames (mean IoU 0.962); Confirm F1 was 0.894 for CSP and 0.819 for LV. Deterministic geometry met both biometric tolerances in 91.6% frames versus 84.1% for segmentation, reducing BPD MAE by 0.291 mm (95% CI 0.225–0.355) and improving joint-tolerance performance by 7.5pp (95% CI 5.2–9.9), meaning measurements following positive Confirm being more accurate. Externally, Find localized 99.9% (FP) and 100% (UCL) of frames, with deterministic geometry measurement performing better on FP (91.2%) and segmentation on UCL (79.6%). Site-specific adaptation improved localization but reduced biometry accuracy, which aggregation partially restored. The most memory-intensive ATLAS pathway required 16.50 MB and 57.32 ms per frame. Conclusions This study presents a compact, evidence-traceable framework that treats operationalizing selected ISUOG-relevant anatomical and biometric requirements as computational quality-control states. The system achieves performance comparable to existing approaches, while prioritizing measurement validity and transparency as core design principles. These findings underscore the necessity for clinical AI systems to provide not only accurate results but also interpretable and auditable evidence to support trustworthy integration.

title: Methodology of a prospective, single-arm, multicenter, physician-initiated study to assess the long-term safety and efficacy of the Restorer stent system for the treatment of aorto-iliac lesions. BARISTA trial.
abstract: Abstract Background Evidence regarding optimal stent selection in endovascular treatment of aorto-iliac lesions remains inconclusive, particularly in complex TASC C and D disease. Interpretation of existing data is complicated by study heterogeneity and selection bias. Both bare metal stents (BMS) and covered stents (CS) are widely used, yet comparative evidence remains limited. The BARISTA trial aims to prospectively evaluate the safety and efficacy of the Restorer iliac stent system (iVascular) and to compare its outcomes with those reported in contemporary studies assessing covered stents. Methods Between July 2022 and June 2024, this prospective multicenter study enrolled 200 patients across 14 Belgian centers. The objective is to assess two-year safety and efficacy outcomes of the Restorer iliac stent system in symptomatic aorto-iliac disease. The primary composite endpoint includes: (1) freedom from target lesion revascularization (TLR), (2) freedom from major amputation, and (3) absence of restenosis within 12 months. TLR is defined as any repeat intervention within the treated segment, including 5 mm proximal and distal to the lesion. Restenosis is defined as > 50% stenosis on duplex ultrasound with a systolic velocity ratio > 2.4. Discussion By analyzing outcomes in a large prospective cohort and comparing results with contemporary CS data, the BARISTA trial aims to support evidence-based stent selection in aorto-iliac disease. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT05293002 (2022-03-23)

title: A Study on the Application of Multimodal MRI Deep Learning in the Early Detection of Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head
abstract: Abstract Objective: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) is a debilitating disorder that frequently leads to hip joint dysfunction. Early and accurate diagnosis is crucial to improving clinical outcomes. This study aimed to develop a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based detection model using the You Only Look Once (YOLO) deep learning framework for automatic identification of early-stage ONFH, and to systematically evaluate how different MRI modalities affect detection performance and their potential for clinical decision support. Methods: We retrospectively collected MRI data from 253 ONFH patients across two medical centers, including T1-weighted Imaging (T1WI) and T2-weighted Imaging (T2WI) sequences. After standardized preprocessing, the dataset was partitioned into training, validation, and test sets (7:1:2). Two sequential experiments were conducted. Experiment 1 compared six YOLO generations (v3, v5, v8, v10, v11, v13) using single-center T1WI data, with precision (P), recall (R), mean average precision (mAP), and inference speed as primary metrics. Experiment 2 applied the optimal model to single-modality (T1WI or T2WI) and multimodal fused images from both centers, using the same metrics to quantify detection efficacy and validate multicenter robustness. Results: In Experiment 1, YOLO v11 outperformed all other models, achieving a mAP@0.5 of 0.966, a recall of 0.941, and a per-frame inference time of 4.9 ms. In Experiment 2, the multimodal fusion input (T1WI+T2WI) yielded the highest performance across all modalities, with a mAP@0.5 of 0.9637, a recall of 0.9388, and the fastest inference time (3.0 ms), surpassing both T1WI (R=0.9159, 4.9 ms) and T2WI (R=0.9113, 6.0 ms) alone. Conclusion: The proposed YOLO v11 model demonstrates excellent performance in MRI-based ONFH detection, and the multimodal fusion strategy further improves both diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency. This approach addresses the dual clinical requirements for high precision and real-time processing, offering a practical and objective intelligent tool for early ONFH screening.

title: Material selection for a 3D-printed tissue-equivalent cost-effective phantom for radiotherapy quality assurance
abstract: Abstract Background and Aims: Patient-specific 3D-printed phantoms are increasingly used for radiotherapy quality assurance (QA) because they are cost-effective and reproduce individual patient anatomy. A major challenge is identifying materials that mimic human tissue.In this work we systematically evaluate radiological properties of various commonly available and industrial 3D printing materials, whereby we include a combined characterization at diagnostic (keV) and therapeutic (MeV) photon energies. Methods and Materials: Over 60 cubes of plastic samples of about 30 materials and different in-fill densities were printed using three different filament printers. CT scans were acquired and the average Hounsfield Units (HU) for each sample was determined. Massdensities (ρm), electron density (ρe), and relative electron density (RED) were assessed. All samples were compared with ICRU reference data. The response at therapeutic energies was evaluated by irradiating the samples and measuring the deposited dose using a micro-diamond detector. These were compared with Pinnacle TPS predictions. Results: The tested materials with 100% filling showed HU values between -95.52 and 238.63. The ρm, ρe, and RED values ranged from 0.963 to 1.228 g/cm3, 3.128 to 3.898 ×1023 and 0.935 to 1.166, respectively. Deviations between measured and TPS dose ranged from -1.34% to 1.36%. Several materials matched ICRU soft-tissue specification. By varying the in-fill density of the materials, refinements could be realized. Conclusions: By combining CT-based characterization with MeV dosimetric validation and testing materials from multiple printing technologies, we identified several candidate plastics suitable for soft-tissue-equivalent radiotherapy phantoms. These can be printed using moderately priced 3D printers (<∼5k euro).

title: Associations of initial blood gas parameters with post-cooling MRI-derived brain volumes and Rutherford injury scores in neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy: a retrospective exploratory study
abstract: Abstract Background Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may reveal structural alterations not captured by conventional visual assessment in neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE). This study investigated associations between initial blood gas parameters and post-cooling MRI-derived brain volumes and Rutherford MRI injury scores in neonates treated with therapeutic hypothermia. Methods This retrospective exploratory study included 79 neonates with HIE. Initial pH, partial pressure of carbon dioxide, bicarbonate, base excess, and lactate were evaluated in relation to 50 absolute MRI-derived brain-volume measures and the consensus Rutherford score. Associations were assessed using Spearman correlations and separate multivariable linear regression models adjusted for gestational age at birth, postnatal age at MRI, and sex, with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Two blinded radiologists independently assigned Rutherford scores and resolved disagreements by consensus. Secondary analyses compared neonates with pH ≤ 7.00 and pH > 7.00. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controlled the false discovery rate within prespecified analysis families. Results Consensus Rutherford scores were available for all 79 neonates (mean, 6.91 ± 1.34; median, 7; interquartile range, 6–8; range, 4–9). Interobserver agreement was good (absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficient, 0.789; quadratic-weighted κ, 0.787); exact agreement occurred in 50.6% of examinations, and scores differed by no more than 1 point in 88.6%. After false-discovery-rate correction, no initial blood gas parameter was significantly associated with the consensus Rutherford score in either unadjusted or adjusted analyses. The adjusted mean score difference between the pH groups was−0.20 (95% confidence interval,−0.93 to 0.54; p = 0.597). No blood gas–volume association remained significant after correction, and no absolute or intracranial-volume-normalized measure differed significantly between the pH groups. Conclusions This exploratory cohort provided no evidence of associations between initial blood gas parameters and post-cooling Rutherford MRI injury scores or global and regional brain volumes after correction for multiple comparisons. These findings do not exclude clinically relevant associations and require confirmation in larger studies using neonatal-validated segmentation methods.

title: Deep Learning Trained Without Target-Domain Labels Improves Risk Stratification Over Expert Coronary Calcium Reading on Routine Attenuation Correction CT
abstract: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) is an established measure of coronary atherosclerosis on computed tomography (CT). Many SPECT and most PET myocardial perfusion studies already include a low-dose CT scan from which coronary calcium could be reported, yet it almost never is. CAC may not be reported due to image noise, cardiac motion, or the absence of a reliable reference standard. Deep learning (DL) models trained on these low-dose CT scans inherit the same uncertainty, because their reference labels are drawn on the degraded images. We bypassed this limitation by training a DL CAC model entirely outside the target domain: expert labels from high-quality gated CT were inherited by synthetic ungated images derived from those same scans, so that no CTAC scan was annotated, and no real CTAC image was used, at any point in training. Models were trained using one center and externally tested in two other centers. Because each synthetic image is derived from the gated scan itself, expert gated segmentations remain valid voxel-for-voxel without registration. Using these pairs, we developed a cross-domain knowledge adaptation model (knowledge adaptation, KAD-CAC). The DL models were externally tested on 5969 patients with a median age of 64 (IQR 56 - 73), of whom 50.2% were male. The KAD-CAC model had higher Cohens kappa K (0.86, 95% CI 0.84 - 0.88) compared to a convolutional LSTM model (K 0.78, 95% CI 0.76 - 0.80, p<0.01), or models trained with only gated images (K 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 - 0.82, p<0.01). Net reclassification improvement for death or myocardial infarction over a clinical and perfusion baseline was greatest for the KAD-CAC model and exceeded that of expert CAC reading on the same CTAC scans (difference 0.089, 95% CI 0.051 to 0.125, p<0.001). A model trained without any labels from CTAC scans therefore stratified risk of death or MI better than expert reading of the same scans. Patients classified as CAC 0 by KAD-CAC had lower adjusted risk of death or MI than patients classified as CAC 0 by experts (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.25 - 0.98). We use paired synthetic ungated scans to transfer expert gated CAC annotations into the ungated domain, resulting in better vessel-level CAC scoring and improved risk reclassification compared with expert reading of the same scans. Automated CAC scoring could be added to every myocardial perfusion imaging report without additional imaging or radiation. The approach provides a general route to expert-quality supervision for any acquisition in which the native reference standard is unreliable.

title: Ascending Aortic Calcium Identifies Patients at Risk Despite Normal Myocardial Flow, Perfusion and Coronary Calcium: A 13-Site Cohort Study
abstract: Background Patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve (MFR) and no coronary artery calcium (CAC) on myocardial perfusion imaging are considered low risk. Yet, adverse events still occur and no routinely reported imaging marker stratifies residual risk. This study aims to determine whether fully automated ascending aortic calcification (AAC) from the attenuation correction CT stratifies risk in these patients. Methods In the multicenter REFINE-PET registry, AAC was quantified from non-contrast CT using deep learning aortic segmentation and Agatston scoring. Triple-normal was defined as stress total perfusion deficit (TPD) <5%, MFR >2 and CAC 0. The primary endpoint was cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission, with heart failure admission as key secondary endpoint. Cox models were adjusted for clinical confounders. Results Of 21,923 patients, 3,580 (16.3%) were triple-normal, of whom 1,322 (36.9%) had AAC (median Agatston 65, IQR 22-212). Agreement with three blinded readers was good to excellent (Intraclass correlation coefficient 0.87-0.90). Over a median follow-up of 52 months (IQR 26-69), 194 primary events occurred. Per standard deviation, AAC was independently associated with the primary endpoint (adjusted HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40; p<0.001), heart failure admission (adjusted HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.10-1.55; p=0.003) and all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04-1.32; p=0.009). AAC improved model fit beyond clinical factors, MFR and TPD (p≤0.009), with modest gains in discrimination (ΔC 0.007-0.009). Conclusions In patients with normal PET readouts, automated AAC was independently associated with adverse outcomes, most strongly heart failure admission, beyond clinical risk factors, perfusion and flow. Clinical Perspective What Is New? In 3,580 patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve and no coronary artery calcium on PET, more than one in three had ascending aortic calcification on the attenuation correction CT. Ascending aortic calcification was independently associated with cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission (adjusted hazard ratio per SD 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40), most strongly with heart failure admission. A fast, fully automated method scored ascending aortic calcification with agreement to expert readers similar to agreement between readers. What Are the Clinical Implications? A normal perfusion PET with normal flow and no coronary calcium does not mean uniformly low risk when the ascending aorta is calcified. Because ascending aortic calcification is scored automatically from the CT acquired with every perfusion PET, it could be reported routinely without additional scanning, cost or radiation. Patients presumed low risk who have ascending aortic calcification may warrant heart failure-oriented prevention, such as natriuretic peptide screening, pending prospective validation.

Per standard deviation, AAC was independently associated with the primary endpoint (adjusted HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40; p<0.001), heart failure admission (adjusted HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.10-1.55; p=0.003) and all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04-1.32; p=0.009). AAC improved model fit beyond clinical factors, MFR and TPD (p≤0.009), with modest gains in discrimination (ΔC 0.007-0.009).

Conclusions

In patients with normal PET readouts, automated AAC was independently associated with adverse outcomes, most strongly heart failure admission, beyond clinical risk factors, perfusion and flow.

Clinical Perspective

What Is New?

In 3,580 patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve and no coronary artery calcium on PET, more than one in three had ascending aortic calcification on the attenuation correction CT. Ascending aortic calcification was independently associated with cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission (adjusted hazard ratio per SD 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40), most strongly with heart failure admission. A fast, fully automated method scored ascending aortic calcification with agreement to expert readers similar to agreement between readers.

What Are the Clinical Implications?

A normal perfusion PET with normal flow and no coronary calcium does not mean uniformly low risk when the ascending aorta is calcified. Because ascending aortic calcification is scored automatically from the CT acquired with every perfusion PET, it could be reported routinely without additional scanning, cost or radiation. Patients presumed low risk who have ascending aortic calcification may warrant heart failure-oriented prevention, such as natriuretic peptide screening, pending prospective validation.

title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI
abstract: ABSTRACT Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI. Graphical Abstract

title: BaT-SAM: Introducing Inductive Bias into SAM via a Mixture of Convolutional Experts for Brain Tumor Segmentation
abstract: Accurate brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning; however, manual delineation is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Existing approaches are either task-specific with limited generalization or rely on user-provided prompts during inference. We present BaT-SAM, a parameter-efficient adaptation framework that enables fully automatic brain tumor segmentation with the Segment Anything Model (SAM). BaT-SAM injects local inductive bias into SAM's frozen Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder via Conv-LoRA, where image features are processed by a sparsely gated mixture of multi-scale convolutional experts. This design compensates for the limited translation-equivariant inductive bias of vanilla ViTs while fine-tuning fewer than 5M parameters (less than 1% of the full model). To remove the need for user prompts, we further introduce a lightweight self-prompting box regressor that is jointly optimized with the adapter using scheduled sampling and predicts tumor locations directly from image embeddings. On the BRISC2025 benchmark, BaT-SAM achieves a weighted mean IoU of 0.832 while outperforming state-of-the-art benchmarks. It further demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization, achieving Dice scores of 0.702 on Figshare and 0.784 on the LGG MRI Segmentation dataset.

title: Lesion-Aware Attention for Mammography Segmentation with Heterogeneous Supervision
abstract: Accurate lesion segmentation in mammography is important for computer-aided breast cancer diagnosis, but dense pixel-level annotations remain costly and limited. Existing public segmentation datasets usually cover only a small set of lesion types with manually delineated masks, whereas larger mammography datasets often provide only image-level diagnostic labels. This annotation mismatch makes it difficult to train segmentation models that can generalize to rare or weakly annotated lesion categories. To address this problem, we study open-vocabulary mammographic lesion segmentation under a mixed-supervision setting, where pixel-level masks are available for base lesion categories and image-level labels are available for a broader set of categories. We propose a two-branch framework that jointly learns from segmentation data and classification data. The segmentation branch learns lesion boundaries from annotated masks, while the classification branch introduces additional image-level semantic supervision. To better transfer image-level supervision to lesion-relevant regions, we further introduce a Lesion-wise Attentive Classifier that maintains category-specific feature prototypes and generates lesion-aware attention maps for foreground feature pooling. This design reduces the influence of background tissue and encourages more compact lesion representations. Experiments on multiple mammography datasets show that the proposed method consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation baselines on both base and novel lesion categories, while reducing the gap to fully supervised models that require dense target-domain masks. Qualitative results further indicate that our method produces more complete lesion localization for small, low-contrast, and visually subtle mammographic findings.

title: Transcutaneous Skin Perforation by a Protruding Xiphoid Process in a Bedbound Patient With Post-Traumatic Cervical Myelopathy: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
abstract: Abstract Background The xiphoid process is the smallest and most morphologically variable component of the sternum, and anterior (ventral) deviation is a recognized anatomical variant. Symptomatic xiphoid disease typically presents as localized pain (xiphodynia). Cutaneous complications are exceedingly uncommon, and only a single previous report describing an ischemic xiphisternal ulcer associated with a protruding xiphoid has been published. To the best of our knowledge, we identified no previous English-language report describing complete transcutaneous perforation of the skin by a protruding xiphoid process associated with chronic sinus formation and secondary infection. Case presentation A 71-year-old bedbound man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and post-traumatic cervical myelopathy with spastic weakness developed progressive protrusion of the xiphoid process. The angulated xiphoid tip gradually eroded through the overlying skin, producing a chronic midline ulcer with sinus tract formation and superimposed infection. Lateral radiography demonstrated marked anterior angulation of the xiphoid process with prominent ventral protrusion and irregularity of the distal tip. The patient underwent xiphoidectomy with en-bloc excision of the ulcer and debridement of devitalized soft tissue. Intraoperative culture of the resected xiphoid specimen yielded extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli, and culture-directed carbapenem therapy was administered. Histopathological examination revealed extensive ulceration with inflamed granulation tissue and a sinus tract, accompanied by reactive squamous epithelial hyperplasia (pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia), whereas the underlying bone was unremarkable and showed no evidence of malignancy. Conclusions A protruding xiphoid process can rarely progress beyond pain and superficial ulceration to cutaneous breach with sinus tract formation and secondary infection, particularly in debilitated patients with chronic immobility, diabetes mellitus, and reduced soft-tissue padding. This process appears mechanistically analogous to a pressure ulcer developing over an atypical bony prominence. Xiphoidectomy combined with debridement and culture-directed antimicrobial therapy appears to provide definitive treatment. Histopathological examination is essential because reactive pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia at the ulcer margin may mimic cutaneous malignancy.

title: Cephalothoracoomphalopagus Tetrabrachius Tetrapus Conjoined Twins: An Extremely Rare Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Conjoined twins are a rare subset of monozygotic twins that usually have a poor prognosis, which has become a significant cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality. This case highlights the importance of routine antenatal care for earlier prenatal diagnosis and well-informed family counseling concerning appropriate intervention for conjoined twins. Case presentation: A 31-year-old G2P1 female in 29 4/7 weeks of gestation was referred from a primary health care center to our hospital with conjoined twins. Two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) ultrasonography examinations at 29 4/7 weeks of gestation revealed one fetal head accompanied by an orbital hypotelorism with an interocular diameter of 0.99 cm. The liver and heart were found to be the fusion organs involved. Polyhydramnios was observed with a maximum vertical pocket of 12.07 cm. Diagnosis of cephalo-thoraco-omphalopagus conjoined twins was made right after the first scan and consistently confirmed thereafter by six more repeated ultrasound examinations. Clinical examination after scheduled surgical delivery in 33 5/7 weeks old neonates revealed male conjoined twins with a fused head accompanied by two pairs of ears, along with a single trunk together with four neurologically independent upper limbs and lower limbs, as well as two complements of genitalia and two anuses. The twin showed signs of respiratory distress and died within one hour of birth. Conclusion Routine antenatal care and advanced ultrasound scanning are crucial for earlier prenatal diagnosis and well-informed family counseling concerning appropriate intervention for conjoined twins.

title: A novel sub-junctional pinhole technique (S-PHT) in treating intrabony defects of stage III periodontitis – Case Series
abstract: Abstract Background Sub-junctional pinhole technique (S-PHT) is a minimally invasive approach in which graft material is introduced into the intrabony defect through a pinhole made on the facial surface opposite to the intrabony defect alveolar crest and apical to the junctional epithelium 4 weeks following minimally invasive non-surgical therapy. This strategy is intended to keep the long junctional epithelium as a biologic seal over the grafted material, while providing maximum soft tissue support around the grafted material. Methods This case series presents the short-term outcome of ten patients diagnosed with stage III grade A periodontitis with interproximal intrabony defects of at least 3 mm, treated with S-PHT. Xenogenic graft material was introduced into the defect through a facial pinhole opposite to the alveolar crest following defect degranulation using minimally invasive hand and ultrasonic instrumentation. Clinical and radiographic parameters were recorded at baseline (4 weeks after non-surgical therapy) and at 9 months following S-PHT. Results Nine months following S-PHT, all sites measured ≤ 4mm probing pocket depth (PPD). The number of sites with clinical attachment level (CAL) gain ≥ 3mm was 6 out of the 10 reported cases. Six sites out of the 10 cases fulfilled a composite outcome of pocket closure of ≤ 4 mm with ≥ 3 mm attachment gain and no bleeding on probing. Significant improvement in intrabony defect fill reported after 9 months with a mean defect fill of 3.1 mm (< 0.001). Conclusions This case series demonstrates that S-PHT, as a minimally invasive approach, could be a reliable patient friendly option for treating intrabony defects in stage III periodontitis. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov. identifiers NCT07763223 PRT-RCT-2026-001 (05-08-2026 and retrospectively registered 19-08-2026)

title: A Decade-Old Retained Intrapleural Glass Fragment in an Asymptomatic Skydiver: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
abstract: Abstract Retained intrathoracic foreign bodies are usually discovered after a traumatic event that the patient clearly remembers. Glass, however, can be especially problematic. It is frequently retained, may be missed during the initial assessment, can appear variably on imaging, and may migrate months or even years after injury rather than becoming securely encapsulated. To our knowledge, an entirely asymptomatic intrapleural glass fragment discovered incidentally in a skydiver has not previously been reported. We describe a 34-year-old male skydiver who was referred after a routine screening chest radiograph showed an abnormal shadow in the right hemithorax. Ten years earlier, he had sustained a penetrating right-sided chest injury during a parachute landing, when he crashed through a window. At that time, he was treated for haemopneumothorax with intercostal drainage, but no foreign body was suspected or actively sought. On current examination, he had a contracted right hemithorax. Computed tomography revealed a radio-dense pleural foreign body. Right-sided thoracotomy was performed, and a 7 × 2.5 cm glass fragment was removed from dense pleural adhesions. His postoperative recovery was uneventful, and he later returned to skydiving.

title: Application Effects of Modified Coronectomy in Mandibular Third Molars with High-Risk Proximity to the Mandibular Canal and Characteristics of Residual Root Migration
abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate the perioperative outcomes, the protective effect on the inferior alveolar nerve, and the migration characteristics of residual roots within 12 months postoperatively following a modified coronectomy in cases of high-risk contact between the mandibular third molar root and the mandibular canal. Materials and Methods The study included 73 patients treated at the Department of Stomatology, First Affiliated Hospital of the Army Medical University, from November 2023 to July 2025. All patients underwent preoperative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans and were divided into three groups based on the surgical procedure performed: the exodontia group (33 patients), the coronectomy group (5 patients), and the modified coronectomy group (35 patients). The primary outcome was postoperative sensation in the lower lip and chin, secondary outcomes included operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative pain, facial swelling, limited mouth opening, temporomandibular joint clicking, and residual root migration. Clinical and radiographic follow-up lasted up to 12 months. Results The operative time in the modified coronectomy group was 51.30 ± 19.63 min, which was longer than the 32.97 ± 13.81 min in the exodontia group (P < 0.001); intraoperative blood loss was 15.07 ± 7.03 mL and 10.42 ± 5.88 mL, respectively (P < 0.05); Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores on postoperative day 3 were 2.50 ± 0.75 and 3.09 ± 1.35, respectively (P < 0.05). No inferior alveolar nerve injury was observed in the modified coronectomy group, whereas the incidence in the exodontia group was 12.12% (P < 0.001); associated sensory abnormalities resolved approximately 3 months postoperatively. Residual root displacement increased with extended follow-up. At 12 months postoperatively, the migration distances for the groups with residual root lengths of ≤ 5 mm, 5–10 mm, and > 10 mm were 4.82 ± 0.59 mm, 3.06 ± 0.81 mm, and 4.13 ± 0.75 mm. After stratification by root morphology, the fusion root group exhibited more pronounced migration in the later stages, while the single-root group showed the lowest migration at 12 months. Conclusion In this study, no inferior alveolar nerve injury was observed in the modified coronectomy group, and postoperative pain scores were low. However, this procedure involved a longer operative time and relatively higher intraoperative blood loss. Residual root migration may be related to residual root length and root morphology, with 5–10 mm residual roots exhibiting relatively better stability during the 12-month follow-up period. Clinical Implications: For mandibular third molars where the root is closely associated with the mandibular canal and complete extraction may increase the risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury, modified coronectomy can serve as an alternative treatment strategy. During surgery, attention should be paid to the complete removal of enamel, control of residual root length, and preservation of alveolar bone, and standardized postoperative follow-up should be implemented.

Residual root migration may be related to residual root length and root morphology, with 5–10 mm residual roots exhibiting relatively better stability during the 12-month follow-up period. Clinical Implications: For mandibular third molars where the root is closely associated with the mandibular canal and complete extraction may increase the risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury, modified coronectomy can serve as an alternative treatment strategy. During surgery, attention should be paid to the complete removal of enamel, control of residual root length, and preservation of alveolar bone, and standardized postoperative follow-up should be implemented.

title: MESNet: A Lightweight Transformer-CNN Collaborative Network with Morphology Awareness for Glioma Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Glioma segmentation is of great significance for clinical diagnosis and treatment, in which the effective utilization of multimodal information is crucial. Accurate segmentation holds substantial clinical value for guiding precise surgical resection, formulating personalized radiotherapy plans, and assessing prognosis. However, most existing methods focus primarily on the extraction and selection of deep semantic features while overlooking morphologically meaningful features such as edges and shapes. To address this issue, we propose a lightweight high-performance network named MESNet (Morphological Edge and Shape Network). MESNet is a Transformer–CNN collaborative segmentation model that explicitly imposes edge consistency and shape regularity to introduce morphological constraints, thereby enabling precise brain tumor segmentation. The model adopts an efficient 3D Transformer as its backbone, organically integrating convolutional neural networks to capture local details. Through deep complementarity between global context and fine-grained representations, it achieves accurate segmentation. To strengthen boundary awareness, a lightweight multi-scale edge-aware module is designed, which utilizes Sobel-based edge enhancement and spatial attention mechanisms to explicitly sharpen tumor boundaries, substantially reducing boundary errors without significantly increasing computational overhead. To accommodate irregular tumor morphology, an attention-guided shape-aware module is constructed; a zero-initialization strategy is employed to maintain training stability, and the module adaptively focuses on variations in tumor scale and shape, markedly improving the segmentation completeness and contour adherence of small targets such as enhancing tumors. Meanwhile, the network adheres to a lightweight design philosophy, strictly controlling parameter counts and computational complexity through channel compression and efficient attention mechanisms. Experimental results on the BraTS2021 dataset demonstrate that MESNet achieves overall segmentation accuracy and boundary agreement comparable to those of state-of-the-art methods while consuming substantially fewer resources, attaining a superior balance between efficiency and performance. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/tanjia123456/MESNet-main.

title: Primary malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor of the vagina: a rare case report
abstract: Abstract Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) is an aggressive sarcoma typically arising from major nerve trunks in the trunk or extremities. Primary MPNST of the vagina is exceptionally rare, with very few cases reported in the literature to date. Herein, we report a rare case of a 67-year-old woman presenting with an 8-month history of vaginal bleeding and fluid discharge. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a solid mass (50*40*36 mm) on the posterior vaginal wall. The tumor was completely removed via radical surgical intervention, and the diagnosis of vaginal MPNST was confirmed through pathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis. Although adjuvant radiotherapy was recommended postoperatively based on clinical guidelines, the patient did not undergo this treatment. At the 3-month follow-up, gynecological examination and ultrasonography showed no signs of recurrence. However, one year after surgery, the patient presented with anal pain and discomfort. Pelvic MRI and CT demonstrated extensive recurrent masses in the pelvis and perineum, involving the rectum and anal canal with suspected anal fistula. Systemic evaluation indicated recurrence involving the posterior bladder wall and distal left ureter, resulting in mild left hydronephrosis, along with suspected metastasis to the right hepatic lobe. This case highlights the highly aggressive nature of primary vaginal MPNST and underscores the critical importance of adjuvant therapy and rigorous long-term surveillance for this extremely rare malignancy.

title: Intraoperative Inhalation of Indocyanine Green for Near-Infrared Visualization of Adult Intralobar Pulmonary Sequestration
abstract: Abstract Background The border between sequestered and normal lung in intralobar pulmonary sequestration (ILS) is often indistinct, complicating precise resection. Intravenous indocyanine green (ICG) can outline a perfusion-based boundary but requires prior control of the aberrant systemic artery and does not directly reflect the airway isolation that defines ILS. Case Presentation : Four adults with contrast-enhanced CT-confirmed ILS underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with intraoperative unilateral ICG inhalation. After single-lung ventilation, aerosolized ICG (2.5 mg/mL) was delivered via a nebulizer connected to the double-lumen tube for 10 to 15 minutes. Near-infrared thoracoscopy showed homogeneous fluorescence in ventilated normal lung and no fluorescence in sequestered tissue, producing a clear demarcation. Three patients underwent wedge resection; one with extensive basal segment involvement underwent lobectomy. No ICG-related adverse events occurred, and all patients recovered uneventfully. Conclusions Intraoperative aerosolized ICG inhalation safely and directly visualizes the ventilation-based boundary characteristic of adult ILS, enabling early lesion mapping and selection of the least extensive complete resection.

title: Normotension as a Red Flag: A Proposed Framework for Early Recognition of Masked Preeclampsia in Couvelaire Uterus – A Case Report and a Teaching Tool
abstract: Abstract Background Couvelaire uterus (CU) is a rare, life-threatening complication of placental abruption, occurring in about 1% of cases. Preeclampsia is a major risk factor; however, its diagnosis becomes difficult when concealed hemorrhage hides typical hypertension, delaying recognition. Additionally, the critical impact of the time from symptom onset to surgical intervention on uterine preservation is not well understood in the literature. We present a case of CU with masked preeclampsia and evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) to propose a new time-based framework for early recognition and surgical decision-making. Case presentation: We report a 19-year-old unbooked primigravida at 35 + 5 weeks presenting with absent fetal movements. On admission, she was normotensive (110/60 mmHg) with a relative rise in heart rate (HR: 88 bpm), severe proteinuria (1000 mg/dL), thrombocytopenia (78×10⁹/L), and a woody uterus. Coagulation revealed PT 17.7s (INR 1.42) and fibrinogen (3.38 g/L), consistent with non-overt DIC (ISTH score 2/8). Ultrasound confirmed intrauterine fetal demise. Over seven hours, labor did not progress, necessitating emergency cesarean section. Intraoperatively, a retroplacental hematoma and CU were identified, and a prophylactic B-Lynch suture was placed (estimated blood loss 1500–2000 mL). Postoperatively, rebound hypertension to 150/100 mmHg responded promptly to magnesium sulfate, confirming masked PE. She recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day four. Discussion Based on this case, we propose three educational frameworks: (1) a three-phase hemodynamic model (occult compensation, rebound surge, therapeutic stabilization) to unmask PE during hemorrhage; (2) a "window of opportunity" concept, advocating surgical intervention within 6–8 hours of symptom onset to avoid irreversible DIC (ISTH ≥ 5) and preserve the uterus; and (3) a counterfactual analysis of two similar cases, demonstrating that timely intervention is the single most modifiable factor for uterine salvage. Conclusion Normotension in PA with proteinuria is a red flag, not reassurance. Magnesium responsiveness confirms underlying PE. B-Lynch suture is effective for uterine preservation, even in resource-limited settings. Clinicians must prioritize early evacuation, especially in conflict-affected areas.

title: Radiation-Induced High-Grade Glioma in a Long-Term Survivor of Medulloblastoma: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Advances in multimodal therapy have significantly improved survival in medulloblastoma, but long-term survivors remain at risk of secondary malignancies. We describe a rare case of radiation-induced high-grade glioma developing after a disease-free interval of approximately seven years, and nearly nine years following initial treatment. Case Presentation A 19-year-old male with a history of classical medulloblastoma (CNS WHO grade 4) presented nine years after his initial diagnosis with worsening headaches and fatigue. His primary tumor was treated with multiple surgical resections followed by high-dose craniospinal irradiation and adjuvant chemotherapy, after which he remained under surveillance. Seven years after completing treatment, he came in with a four-week history of weight loss and fatigue. One week before admission, he developed drowsiness, followed by a 10-day history of right focal seizures and increasing right-sided weakness. On neurological examination, he was obtunded with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9/15 and showed right-sided spastic hemiparesis with impaired verbal responsiveness. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple supratentorial lesions associated with extensive vasogenic edema and mild midline shift, raising concern for a secondary malignant neoplasm. A left frontal burr-hole biopsy was subsequently performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated a highly cellular glial neoplasm composed of pleomorphic, hyperchromatic tumor cells embedded within a fibrillary background. Prominent microvascular proliferation and frequent mitotic activity were identified, consistent with a high-grade infiltrating glioma. Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) positivity, absence of IDH1 R132H expression, retained ATRX nuclear staining, and a Ki-67 proliferation index of 15–20%. Tumor cells were negative for H3K27M, and mismatch repair protein expression was preserved. Based on the histopathological and immunophenotypic findings, a diagnosis of high-grade glioma, favoring astrocytoma, NOS, CNS WHO grade 4, was established. Given the patient's previous exposure to craniospinal radiotherapy and the prolonged latency period of nine years between treatment of the primary medulloblastoma and development of the high grade glioma, the lesion was highly suggestive of radiation-induced high-grade glioma. Despite supportive management, the patient's clinical condition deteriorated rapidly, and he succumbed to the disease one month after diagnosis. Conclusion This case illustrates the development of a secondary high-grade glioma in a long-term survivor of medulloblastoma, most likely representing a radiation-induced malignancy. It highlights the critical importance of lifelong surveillance in survivors of pediatric brain tumors, as early detection of secondary central nervous system neoplasms may allow timely intervention. Despite the limited therapeutic options available for these aggressive tumors, prompt recognition remains essential to optimize patient management and outcomes.

title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome during enfortumab vedotin therapy: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) are widely used to treat solid malignancies. Enfortumab vedotin (EV) is an effective therapeutic option for advanced urothelial carcinoma. Although EV-associated neurotoxicity is most commonly reported as peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system complications, particularly posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), are rare. We report a case of PRES associated with EV therapy. Case presentation: A man in his 50s underwent right nephroureterectomy for urothelial carcinoma, followed by adjuvant nivolumab therapy. Subsequently, multiple liver metastases developed, and treatment with EV was initiated. One day after EV administration during the second cycle, the patient developed acute visual impairment and altered consciousness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences revealed hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter, predominantly involving both occipital lobes, consistent with PRES. EV was discontinued, and conservative management was initiated. The patient's neurological symptoms improved rapidly, and follow-up MRI demonstrated complete radiological resolution of the lesions. Conclusions In patients who develop visual disturbances, altered mental status, or other central neurological symptoms after treatment with EV, PRES should be considered in the differential diagnosis in addition to brain metastases. Early diagnosis of PRES during EV therapy may prevent irreversible neurological sequelae. Prompt neuroimaging evaluation and appropriate management are essential to achieve favorable outcomes.

title: Preoperative prediction and perioperative risk updating for adjacent vertebral fracture after percutaneous vertebroplasty: development and internal validation of a two-stage prediction strategy
abstract: Abstract Background Adjacent vertebral fracture (AVF) is an important complication after percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP) for osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (OVCF). Existing prediction models frequently combine variables obtained at different clinical time points, which may limit their applicability for preoperative risk assessment. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a strictly preoperative prediction model and to determine whether perioperative cement-distribution information provides additional prognostic value after PVP. Methods We retrospectively included 314 consecutive patients with OVCF who underwent PVP between December 2022 and December 2024 and completed at least 18 months of follow-up. The primary outcome was AVF within 18 months after PVP. Model 1 incorporated six preoperative predictors: age, target vertebral CT Hounsfield units (CT-HU), pre-existing vertebral compression fracture (VCF) count, paraspinal fat infiltration rate (FIR), preoperative sagittal imbalance, and preoperative anterior vertebral compression rate. Model 2 retained these predictors and added cement distribution pattern. Internal validation included 1,000 bootstrap resamples, 100 repetitions of stratified five-fold cross-validation, and fixed stratified 10-fold out-of-fold (OOF) prediction. Discrimination, calibration, Brier score, decision curve analysis, and incremental model performance were evaluated. LASSO and DEXA T-score analyses were performed as sensitivity analyses. Results Among 314 patients, 80 (25.5%) developed AVF within 18 months. In Model 1, older age, lower CT-HU, greater pre-existing VCF burden, higher paraspinal FIR, sagittal imbalance, and greater anterior vertebral compression were independently associated with AVF. The apparent AUC was 0.872, the bootstrap-corrected AUC was 0.857, and the 10-fold OOF AUC was 0.854. After addition of cement distribution, contiguous O-shaped and fragmented patterns were associated with higher AVF odds than bilateral H-shaped distribution. Model 2 improved overall model fit (likelihood-ratio χ²=11.99, P = 0.0025), but the increase in OOF discrimination was small (AUC 0.859; ΔAUC = 0.005, 95% CI − 0.014 to 0.025; P = 0.622). Model 1 OOF risk strata showed observed AVF rates of 6.0%, 25.8%, and 63.2% in the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, respectively. Adding DEXA T-score did not materially improve Model 1. Conclusions A six-predictor preoperative model integrating bone quality, previous fracture burden, paraspinal muscle degeneration, sagittal alignment, and vertebral morphology showed good internal performance for predicting 18-month AVF after PVP. Cement distribution provided additional perioperative prognostic information and improved overall model fit, but only minimally increased discrimination. These findings support a two-stage framework in which preoperative risk is estimated first and subsequently updated using procedural information. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: MV‑Flow imaging for predicting adverse pregnancy outcomes in gestational diabetes mellitus
abstract: Abstract Objectives To assess longitudinal placental vascular index (VI) changes using MV-Flow ultrasound in gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and evaluate its predictive value for adverse perinatal outcomes. Methods We enrolled 112 women with GDM from a prospective cohort of 547 singleton pregnancies screened by 75g OGTT at 24–28 weeks. Diagnosis followed IADPSG criteria; exclusions left 60 with favorable outcomes and 29 with adverse outcomes. VIUp, VIMed, and VIDown were measured in upper, mid, and lower placental regions at 22–27 + 6 and 28–33 + 6 weeks using standardized MV-Flow. We calculated VIMean and ΔVI (third minus second trimester). Conventional Doppler parameters were collected concurrently. Group differences were tested parametrically or nonparametrically. Independent predictors were identified via multivariable logistic regression; model discrimination was assessed by ROC analysis and internally validated with 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Results Pre-pregnancy BMI and fasting OGTT glucose were higher in the adverse-outcome group (both P < 0.05). Third-trimester VIMean (36.6 ± 7.8 vs. 41.7 ± 9.3; P = 0.009) and VIMed (27.3 [27.3–48.7] vs. 34.7 [34.7–54.0]; P = 0.023) were lower in the adverse-outcome group. ΔVI and all Doppler parameters showed no group differences (all P > 0.05). Independent predictors were pre-pregnancy BMI (OR = 1.18; 95% CI: 1.03–1.35; P = 0.016), fasting OGTT glucose (OR = 1.12; 95% CI: 0.99–1.26; P = 0.053), and VIMed.2 (OR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.90–0.98; P = 0.005). The combined model (BMI + fasting OGTT glucose + VIMed.2) had AUC = 0.770 (95% CI: 0.671–0.869), versus 0.718 for BMI alone (ΔAUC = 0.052; DeLong test, P = 0.262). Bootstrap-corrected AUC was 0.743. Conclusions Third-trimester VIMed is significantly lower in GDM pregnancies with adverse outcomes. The model combining pre-pregnancy BMI, fasting OGTT glucose, and VIMed.2 shows moderate predictive ability and stable performance—supporting its use as an adjunctive risk-stratification tool in GDM.

title: Indolent Postoperative Endophthalmitis With Vitreous Metagenomic Detection of Enterobacter hormaechei in an Eye With Central Retinal Vein Occlusion: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Enterobacter hormaechei is a member of the Enterobacter cloacae complex and an emerging multidrug-resistant opportunistic pathogen. Enterobacter endophthalmitis is uncommon and usually aggressive; an indolent postoperative presentation associated with species-level detection of E. hormaechei has not been well characterized. Case presentation: A 68-year-old woman with previous central retinal vein occlusion and retinal laser photocoagulation underwent left cataract surgery. Approximately 1 month later, after postoperative drops had been stopped, she developed ocular symptoms diagnosed as conjunctivitis. Follow-up was irregular, and she re-presented approximately 4 months later with persistent visual loss. At admission, left visual acuity was 0.08 (decimal), intraocular pressure was 13 mmHg, the conjunctiva and anterior chamber were quiet, the intraocular lens was centered, and vitreous opacity was most marked anteriorly. Vitreous DNA metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected E. hormaechei (656 reads; relative abundance, 2.80%); the laboratory categorized the signal as a low-attention finding. Intravitreal ceftazidime (1.0 mg/0.1 mL) and norvancomycin hydrochloride (1.0 mg/0.1 mL) produced no clear improvement after 1 week. Pars plana vitrectomy with silicone-oil tamponade was then performed. At 2 months, the retina was attached, intraocular inflammation was controlled, and best-corrected visual acuity was 0.12 (decimal); residual visual limitation was confounded by ischemic retinal disease. Conclusion Delayed postoperative endophthalmitis may present with little anterior-segment inflammation. Vitreous mNGS can identify unexpected organisms, but a low-abundance result without orthogonal confirmation should be interpreted as supportive rather than definitive evidence of causation. Persistent vitreous opacity despite intravitreal antibiotics may justify vitrectomy for source control, diagnostic sampling, and media clearance.
originalAbstract: Background Enterobacter hormaechei is a member of the Enterobacter cloacae complex and an emerging multidrug-resistant opportunistic pathogen.
